## Overview

Belarusians are an East Slavic ethnic group native to Belarus. They share a common culture, ancestry, history, and traditionally speak the Belarusian language. More than 9 million people proclaim Belarusian ethnicity worldwide, including nearly 7.99 million residents of Belarus. Belarusians also live in Ukraine, Poland, the Russian Federation, Lithuania, the United States, Brazil, Canada, the Baltic states, and EU countries. Their historical territory includes the upper Dnieper River basin and the Sozh, Berezina, Pripyat, and Western Dvina river regions. The majority adhere to Eastern Orthodoxy. The sources provide historical and linguistic information.

## Oral tradition & literature

They mention chronicles of Jan of Czarnków in connection with the phrase “Albae Russiae, Poloczk dicto” in 1381.

## Language & religion

Belarusian and Russian are the two official languages of Belarus. Belarusians traditionally speak Belarusian, and Russian became co-official with Belarusian after the 1995 Belarusian referendum. Historically, Ruthenian, Polish, and Latin were spoken by parts of the Ruthenian nobility, while Ruthenian continued in some official contexts until the late 17th century, when it was replaced by Polish. The majority of Belarusians adhere to Eastern Orthodoxy. The sources also describe Greek Catholics of the Ruthenian Uniate Church, created by the Union of Brest in 1596.

commons_photos.title: Belarusian Types by Mikhail Mikeshin (1877).jpg
commons_photos.description: Art illustration (zincography) "Belarusian Types" (original Russian: «Бѣлорусскіе типы») from the weekly magazine "Pchela" (No. 48, 1877, p. 765). Drawing by Mikhail Mikeshin, facsimile on zinc by S. Krakov. The illustration depicts a Belarusian peasant couple (a man with a rooster and a woman with a basket of eggs) in traditional clothing and bast shoes. The print features a handwritten dedication by the artist to the famous collector of Belarusian folklore, Pavel Sheyn.
